title: Numerical Optimization, First Edition: front matter with preface, dedication and table of contents (Springer free preview)
contribution: First-edition preface and full contents (joint with S. J. Wright). The book is a continuous-optimization text with a stated emphasis on large-scale techniques. It has 18 chapters: unconstrained Chapters 2-11, then constrained theory, two LP chapters and NLP algorithms. There is no chapter on interior methods for NLP, which the preface omits as 'the focus of intense current research', and no derivative-free section. The only sentence about Nocedal alone thanks Byrd (p. 9). The Springer description quoted in the a2-02 card of S010 is this preface's first paragraph (p. 6).
problem_entry: The preface starts from the reader ('a book for people interested in solving optimization problems'): students and practitioners need the capabilities and limitations of algorithms. Five application examples are given. The scope is continuous only; discrete and stochastic optimization are omitted (pp. 6-7).
key_idea: Stated emphasis: large-scale techniques (interior-point, inexact Newton, limited-memory, partial separability, automatic differentiation), with trust-region methods and SQP treated 'more thoroughly than existing texts' (p. 7). Contents (title-level): 18 chapters plus Appendix A. Unconstrained Chapters 2-11 run over book pp. 10-313 and constrained Chapters 12-18 over pp. 314-573. LP gets two chapters (13, 14) between constrained theory (12) and the NLP algorithms (15-18). Newton gets its own chapter (6). Chapter 9 holds L-BFGS, the compact representation and three sections on partial separability, including 'Sparsity vs. Partial Separability'. Interior methods for NLP appear only as subsections (16.7 for QP; 17.2's 'Relationship to Primal-Dual Methods'). No title mentions DFO, noise or filters (pp. 10-19).
assumptions: Prerequisites: linear algebra (including numerical linear algebra) and calculus, with the background in the Appendix. 'Formal mathematical requirements are kept to a minimum'. Modelling is light, and optimality conditions 'thorough but not exhaustive' (pp. 6-8).
proof_devices: Proof policy: major results 'are stated, and in many cases proved, in a rigorous fashion'; proofs can be skipped (p. 8).

Proofs are set apart as subsections ('Proof of Theorem 4.3', 'Proof of Theorem 12.1') and convergence sections are given per method class (3.2, 4.3, 8.4 with global and superlinear BFGS convergence, 14.4) (pp. 11-16; title-level).
'Behavior of the Fletcher-Reeves Method' sits next to 'Global Convergence' in 5.2 (p. 12; title-level, content not read).
experiments: n/a. Simple computer exercises in most chapters, and the stated experience that programming projects teach complexity, memory demands and elegance (p. 7). Software packages are mostly omitted, with pointers to the Moré-Wright Optimization Software Guide and the NEOS Guide (p. 9).
positioning: Other texts are named for omitted or light topics: Dantzig and Fourer-Gay-Kernighan for modelling; Mangasarian and Clarke for optimality conditions; network, integer, stochastic and nonsmooth texts (p. 8). The book claims new algorithms 'not described in earlier textbooks' (p. 7). Acknowledgments: 24 colleagues (card's count), including the team members Gill, Gould, Toint and Waechter; DOE and NSF; JN's thanks to Byrd (p. 9). The Final Remark quotes Fletcher's 'fascinating blend of theory and computation, heuristics and rigor' (p. 9).
writing: Conversational style; 'comparatively long' by design. Chapter template: nonrigorous opening with figures, then motivated and explicitly stated algorithms, then rigorous results. The preface has labelled sections (Audience; Emphasis and Writing Style; Topics Not Covered; Additional Resource; Acknowledgments; Final Remark) (pp. 7-9). Comparison: the two a2-02 S010 abstract quotes are verbatim from p. 6.
limits_future: Not covered: network, integer, stochastic, nonsmooth and global optimization. Interior methods for NLP and complementarity algorithms are omitted as current research (p. 8), though both authors had open work on the former (reference list, B006 pp. 38, 48). Future directions only through Fletcher's ingredients (p. 9).

method_links.note: Stated (1999), with the Research Trajectory constant 'the Byrd partnership': the joint preface's only sentence about JN alone, in the third person, thanks Byrd, 'who has taught him so much about optimization' (p. 9). Nocedal-specific, so it passes exclusivity against Wright. The only Nocedal-specific item in the book material; book evidence is dating and framing, never in a say-do count.

Framing, title-level: partial separability gets three sections and a 'Sparsity vs. Partial Separability' subsection in the chapter with L-BFGS; nonlinear least squares and equations get chapters. Confirms a2-02's metadata-level S010 link. Not exclusive (Wright's Method 6 and his taste mark 6). Joint voice of Nocedal and S. J. Wright (book material); framing/dating only; exclude from say-do counts. Heuristic 10 and Heuristic 9 have their own entries. Other links of this card, framing only (no relation, no entry): Taste mark 3 (large-scale emphasis, p. 7); 02 W1 / Mentor Voice, consistent (proofs kept light, pp. 6, 8); Honest Boundary blind spots (p. 8).

Weak, title-level: an observed behaviour ('Behavior of the Fletcher-Reeves Method') gets a subsection next to 'Global Convergence'; S012 is in the reference list (B006 p. 41). Not exclusive (Wright's Method 2). Joint voice of Nocedal and S. J. Wright (book material); framing/dating only; exclude from say-do counts.

The 1999 map leaves out the authors' own live topic, interior methods for NLP, as 'the focus of intense current research' (p. 8). Overlaps Wright's Heuristic 6, so not exclusive. Joint voice of Nocedal and S. J. Wright (book material).

transferable: Write a 'Topics not covered' section naming the best existing text for each omitted area (p. 8).
Say outright when a topic is left out because it is 'the focus of intense current research' (p. 8).
Use a fixed chapter template: nonrigorous opening with figures, then the motivated algorithm stated explicitly, then rigorous results with skippable proofs (p. 8).
Pair chapters with small programming exercises that expose an algorithm's cost, memory and behaviour (p. 7).
coauthors: Stephen J. Wright (Argonne National Laboratory, MCS Division, p. 4)

quotes.text: We omit some important topics, such as network optimization, integer programming, stochastic programming, nonsmooth optimization, and global optimization.
One of us (JN) would like to express his deep gratitude to Richard Byrd, who has taught him so much about optimization and who has helped him in very many ways throughout the course of his career.

title: Numerical Optimization, First Edition: back matter with Appendix A (Background Material), references and index (Springer free preview)
contribution: First-edition back matter (joint with S. J. Wright): Appendix A, analysis first and then linear algebra, the reverse of the 2006 order; 259 references; the index. Card's counts: Powell is the most-listed author (19), then Moré 16, Toint 14; Nocedal 11, Byrd 11, S. J. Wright 8; the latest dated entry is from 1999. The index has BFGS 'self-correction', complexity only on LP pages, and no filter, noise, DFO or KNITRO entries. The preview already carries three reference corrections of the authors' 2/25/2000 addendum, two pages lower than its page numbers, so it reproduces a later printing (inference).
problem_entry: Background material to make the book self-contained (preface, B005 p. 7). The appendix points to Chapter 2 for rates of convergence (p. 2).
key_idea: A.1 Analysis, Geometry, Topology (pp. 2-18): topology, continuity, derivatives, mean value and implicit function theorems, tangent and normal cones of feasible sets, order notation, scalar root-finding. A.2 Linear Algebra (pp. 18-35): norms, subspaces, eigenvalues and SVD, factorizations (Algorithm A.1, p. 26), Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury, interlacing, floating point, conditioning and stability. Comparison (B001 p. 16, title-level): in 2006 the order is reversed, sequences, rates, convex sets and symmetric indefinite factorization are added, 'Geometry of Feasible Sets' is dropped, and Appendix B is added.
assumptions: Everything in IRn; Hilbert-space extensions omitted (p. 21). Feasible sets mostly algebraic, while the geometric view is weighed (p. 11). Double precision, with unit roundoff 'typically about 10-15' (p. 32).
proof_devices: Small numerical examples verify the definitions (Examples A.1-A.2, pp. 9-10).
The cone property of the tangent cone is proved by rescaling the scalar sequence (p. 12); Cauchy-Schwarz via a nonnegative quadratic in alpha (p. 20).
Cited theorems: implicit function theorem after Lang (p. 10); interlacing theorem from Golub and Van Loan (p. 30).
Practical verdict against the worst-case bound: growth factor 'around 2n-1' in the worst case, yet 'stable for all practical purposes'; no pivoting is 'definitely unstable' (pp. 34-35).
experiments: n/a. Only illustrative well- and ill-conditioned 2x2 systems (pp. 33-34).
positioning: References (pp. 36-48; card's count, dittos assigned to the preceding author): 259 entries; latest dated 1999 ([252]); some still 'to appear' ([121], [258]). By author: Powell 19, Moré 16, Toint 14, Schnabel 12, Nocedal 11, Byrd 11, Griewank 11, Fletcher 10, Gill 10, Gould 10, M. H. Wright 10, S. J. Wright 8. Nocedal's are S007, S002, S019, S020, S014, S039, S012, S034, S008 (OTC report 97/05), S005 and S070 (pp. 38, 40-41, 43, 45, 48). Wright's include his 1997 IPM book and three IPM preprints (pp. 44, 46, 48). DFO only by Brent 1973 [27] (p. 37). The Fletcher-Leyffer filter report [86] is cited (p. 40) but not indexed. Test sets: CUTE [25] and MINPACK-2 [5] (pp. 36-37). Index (pp. 49-60): BFGS 'self-correction, 200' (p. 50); complexity only on LP pages 392-417 (p. 50); 'Robustness, 7' (p. 57); IPM for nonlinear programs only at 411, 510-512 and 526 (p. 56); no filter, noise, derivative-free, Nelder-Mead or KNITRO/NITRO entries.
writing: Each definition is followed by a worked example (pp. 9-10). The floating-point section closes with the adage against differencing similar numbers (p. 33). Conditioning (a property of the problem) is separated from stability (a property of the algorithm), 'and we adhere to them in this book' (pp. 33-34).
limits_future: Background only; no Appendix B in this edition's file. Comparison with B007 p. 7: the reference corrections [26] El Ghaoui, [71] Deuflhard and [234] Quasi-Newton / Nonlinear Programming 3 are already made here (pp. 37, 39, 47). The pages are two lower than the addendum's (586, 610, 612, 620 against 588, 612, 614, 622). The (A.24) '= 0' cannot be checked in this text layer (p. 13). Inference: the preview is a later printing.

method_links.note: Framing, index-level: complexity indexed only on LP pages; the appendix keeps a pessimistic worst-case growth bound in view but draws the practical stability verdict. Consistent with taste warning 3. Not exclusive (Wright's taste mark 1 and Method 2). Joint voice of Nocedal and S. J. Wright (book material); framing/dating only; exclude from say-do counts. Non-Method links of this card: taste mark 4, framing (index 'self-correction' under BFGS, p. 50). Academic Lineage, dating (Powell the most-listed author, pp. 38-46; joint list). Research Trajectory, dating (no DFO, noise or filter topics in 1999, pp. 49-60).

transferable: Follow every definition with a small numerical example the reader can check (pp. 9-10).
When a worst-case bound is pessimistic, state it, state what is observed in practice, and draw the practical verdict explicitly (pp. 34-35).
Separate conditioning (a property of the problem) from stability (a property of the algorithm) before discussing error (pp. 33-34).

quotes.text: In practice, however, large growth factors are rarely observed, so we conclude that Algorithm A.1 is stable for all practical purposes.
We omit details, since all the development of this book takes place in the space IRn, though many of the algorithms can be extended to more general Hilbert spaces.

title: Review of Numerical Optimization (first edition, 1999) by Neculai Curteanu in zbMATH Open, Zbl 0930.65067
contribution: zbMATH review of the first edition by N. Curteanu: the reviewer's voice, routed to peer critique. Purely descriptive, it follows the preface paragraph by paragraph (comparison with B005 pp. 6-9). It drops 'continuous' from the stated goal and gives no evaluation, criticism or error. Its 'light' modelling remark is the preface's own self-description (B005 p. 8), which corrects 05-peer-critique Gaps item 12.
problem_entry: The reviewer frames the book by its goal: a comprehensive description of state-of-the-art optimization techniques (p. 1).
key_idea: The reviewer lists the large-scale emphasis and the topics 'detailedly and comprehensively discussed' (p. 1).
assumptions: n/a (reviewer comments on no assumptions; proofs 'may be skipped', p. 1).
positioning: The reviewer places the book as a two-semester graduate course and for practitioners' self-study, and points to the NEOS Software Guide; there is no comparison with other books (p. 1). Bibliographic data as given: 'xx, 636 p. (1999)' (p. 1).
writing: Comparison with B005 pp. 6-9: near-verbatim restatement of the preface's goal sentence (without 'continuous'), large-scale list, audience, chapter template ('motivated, analyzed' for the preface's 'motivated and discussed'), light modelling and NEOS pointer. The 'Topics not covered' section is not mentioned.
limits_future: No criticism, limitation or error is reported (p. 1). Correction for 05 Gaps item 12: 'light' is the authors' own wording (B005 p. 8), so the review contains no criticism at all.
transferable: Before using a book review as critique, compare it with the book's preface; a review that restates the preface carries no independent judgement (p. 1 against B005 pp. 6-9).
coauthors: n/a (review by Neculai Curteanu, Iasi; the reviewed book is by Nocedal and S. J. Wright)

quotes.text: The main goal of the book is to give a comprehensive description of the most powerful, state-of-the-art techniques for solving optimization problems.
the proposed treatment of the optimization process modelling is light, serving mainly to set the stage for the algorithmic developments.

title: Corrections to First Printing of Nocedal-Wright (Numerical Optimization, first edition; additional corrections noted 2/25/2000)
contribution: The authors' first-printing errata for the first edition (joint), written for the typesetter as ready-to-paste LaTeX passages. Card's count: 35 numbered items plus a 4-item addendum dated 2/25/2000. They restore missing hypotheses (a trust-region characterization; the Broyden-family positive definiteness; 'and bounded' in the simplex termination theorem) and fix the simplex chapter's unbounded case (11 of 35 items). Heuristic 7 evidence (a second errata list besides the 80-item 2006 list), shared with Wright's Heuristic 5. The page numbers run two ahead of the Springer preview from Chapter 13 on.
problem_entry: Corrections to the first printing: 35 numbered items (pp. 1-6) and 4 additional items (p. 7), citing book pp. 24-408 and 588-622.
key_idea: List design: for the typesetter, explicit 'corrected sentence' passages to cut and paste from the LaTeX source (p. 1); Procedure 13.1 given 'verbatim' for the source file (p. 6). Kinds (card's classification): cross-references (book pp. 49, 171, 221); signs, inequalities and indices (book pp. 24, 79, 90-91, 118, 408); wording and typography; two deleted sentences in the AD section plus 'exact' changed to 'analytic' (book pp. 176, 180); substantive statements.
assumptions: Missing hypotheses restored: 'p* is feasible and' in the trust-region characterization (book p. 78; p. 2); a two-sided bound on the Broyden parameter for positive definiteness (book p. 208; p. 3; OCR symbols unreliable); 'and bounded' in Theorem 13.4 (book p. 377; p. 6); a new Theorem 13.2 (iii) on feasible bounded LPs (book p. 371; p. 5).
proof_devices: New liminf equation and an outlined proof by contradiction via Zoutendijk's condition for methods such as CG (book p. 46; p. 1).
Inequality directions fixed in the trust-region radius argument (book pp. 90-91; p. 2).
Closedness proof for the set N replaced by a proof under LICQ; a more general argument due to Mangasarian and Schumaker is mentioned and omitted (book p. 357; p. 4).

Simplex chapter rewritten for the unbounded case: Section 13.3's opening, the ratio-test bullet, an unboundedness STOP in Procedure 13.1, and the termination theorem tied to Theorem 13.2 (iii) (book pp. 372-378; pp. 5-6).
Distribution (card's count): Ch. 13: 11; Ch. 7: 7; Ch. 4: 4; Chs. 2, 3, 8: 3 each; Ch. 12: 2; Chs. 5, 14: 1 each; none for Chs. 6, 9-11, 15-18 (pp. 1-6).
positioning: No finder of any error is named (pp. 1-7). Comparison: the 2006 preface thanks readers who sent corrections by name (B001 p. 22). Link (no Method N): Heuristic 7, evidence (joint; not exclusive, Wright's Heuristic 5; exclude from say-do counts).
writing: Imperative edit instructions with line positions counted from either end of the page (p. 3). One first-person singular hedge in the addendum ('I think'), writer not identified, and a remark on the typesetting of 'fl' (p. 7). Undated at the top; the addendum is dated 2/25/2000 (p. 7).
limits_future: OCR: words clean, symbols and subscripts unreliable; some item numbers lost and reconstructed (pp. 2, 6). Nothing says which later printing absorbed which item (see B008, c5-03). Comparison with the preview: page numbers agree through Chapter 8 (book pp. 49, 78, 176, 208 against B005 pp. 11, 13) but run two ahead from Chapter 13 (372/370, 374/372, 393/391; the addendum 588/586, 612/610, 614/612, 622/620; B005 pp. 15-16, B006 pp. 13, 37, 39, 47). The three legible reference corrections are already in the preview. Inference: the preview is a later printing; zbMATH's 'xx, 636 p.' (B009 p. 1) against the preview's last page 634 (B006 p. 60) fits.

method_links.note: A second, earlier errata list: 35 numbered items and a dated addendum of 4, written as replacement passages ready to paste (pp. 1, 6-7). Not exclusive: Wright's Heuristic 5 (keep public errata) covers it. Joint voice (book material); dating only; exclude from say-do counts.

transferable: Publish errata as replacement passages ready to paste into the source, with line positions counted from the top or the bottom of the page (pp. 1, 3, 6).
When a theorem lacks a case (unbounded LP), fix the statement, the algorithm box and the proof together, and say which result proves which (pp. 5-6).
Date the addenda to an errata list (p. 7).

Add a third item to this theorem: “(iii) If (13.1) is feasible and bounded, then it has an optimal solution.”

title: Numerical Optimization, Second Edition: front matter with prefaces, dedications and table of contents (Springer free preview)
contribution: Second-edition front matter (joint with S. J. Wright). New chapters on DFO (9, opening with 'Finite Differences and Noise') and on interior methods for NLP (19), which 'now forms the basis of successful codes'. Newton's method is spread through the unconstrained part, common SQP/IPM material moves to Chapter 15, and filters, SLQP, a penalty-update subsection and six 'Perspectives and Software' sections are added. Reduced-Hessian SQP and partial separability shrink (title-level). The constrained part grows from 260 to 294 pages (card's count). The 1999 preface is reprinted verbatim, and the not-covered list adds MPCC, SOCP/SDP, simulation-based, robust and MINLP.
problem_entry: Why a new edition: the field 'has continued to grow and evolve'; a better understanding of constrained optimization at the algorithmic and theoretical levels and of practical demands (p. 21).
key_idea: Stated changes (pp. 21-22): DFO (Ch. 9) and IPM for NLP (Ch. 19); the unconstrained part reorganized, with Newton distributed rather than 'isolated in a single chapter'; Chapter 7 expanded for large-scale problems; SQP/IPM common material in Ch. 15; primal barrier moved to Ch. 19; duality, inequality QP, dual simplex and presolve, CG for QP, filters and nonsmooth penalties; Perspectives and Software sections. Contents check (comparison with B005, title-level): Newton in 3.4, 4.4 and 7.1 (pp. 8-10); Maratos, SOC and watchdog in 15.5-15.6 (p. 13); log-barrier in 19.6 (p. 16); 'Merit Functions and Filters' 15.4 (p. 13); Perspectives and Software in 7.5, 14.4, 16.8, 17.5, 18.8 and 19.9. Unstated (title-level): reduced-Hessian SQP cut from a section with 4 subsections plus a rate subsection to one subsection (p. 15; B005 p. 18); partial separability from 3 sections to 1 (p. 10; B005 p. 14); coordinate descent moved from Ch. 3 into DFO 9.3; rates moved from Ch. 2 to App. A.2; SLQP and 'A Technique for Updating the Penalty Parameter' in 18.5 (p. 15); both line-search and trust-region IPMs; 19.7 'Failure of the Line Search Approach' (p. 16). Whether these present S042's steering or S061's example is not read. DFO order: finite differences and noise, model-based, coordinate/pattern, conjugate-direction, Nelder-Mead, implicit filtering (pp. 10-11). Balance (card's count): unconstrained 294 pages (1999: 304), constrained 294 (1999: 260).
assumptions: The reprinted 1999 preface is identical to the first edition's except for reference numbers and the spelling of Wachter (card's letter-by-letter comparison with B005 pp. 6-9), so it still omits IPM for NLP (p. 19), which the second preface supersedes (p. 21). The appendix is to be usable 'in a more stand-alone fashion' (p. 22).
proof_devices: Title-level: constrained theory expanded with 12.2 'Tangent Cone and Constraint Qualifications', 12.4 '...: Proof' with Farkas' Lemma, and 12.9 'Duality' (p. 12).

New convergence subsections: local convergence of inexact Newton (p. 10); Gauss-Newton and Levenberg-Marquardt convergence (p. 11); 18.7 Convergence Analysis (p. 15); 19.7-19.8 global and superlinear convergence of IPMs (p. 16).
experiments: n/a. Exercises revised in most chapters; a solutions manual for instructors (p. 22). 'Numerical Performance' now follows 'Global Convergence' in 5.2 (p. 9; B005 p. 12).
positioning: Readers of the first edition who sent corrections are thanked by name: Curtis, Ferris, Griewank, Gondzio, Leyffer, Loewen, Reemtsen, Stewart. Overton 'taught from a draft'. Chapter readers include Byrd, Gould, Hovland, Lopez-Calva, Hei, Scheinberg, Wachter and Waltz (p. 22). No own paper is named as the source of any change (pp. 21-22). a2-02's 'own lines' reading of the new chapters stays an inference, and for IPM it applies to both authors (B006 pp. 38, 48).
writing: Closes the list of changes with the selection sentence (p. 22). Promises a typo list on the web pages of both authors (p. 22). The 1999 preface is kept verbatim and the changes go in a separate preface (pp. 17-22).
limits_future: Not covered, added: 'optimization problems with complementarity constraints, second-order cone and semidefinite programming, simulation-based optimization, robust optimization, and mixed-integer nonlinear programming'; the book 'provides a foundation from which they can be studied' (p. 22). Dating: Nocedal's 2008-2013 complementarity side line lies in an excluded area. The preface says 'six years' since the first edition (p. 21), against the 2026 interview's 'within five years' (06, caption-derived).

method_links.note: Framing, title-level: a named failure followed by the modified methods (19.7 'Failure of the Line Search Approach', 'Modified Line Search Methods'); 1999 had 'Failure of the Active-Set Method' (B005 p. 17). Content not read; whether it is S061's example is unknown. Not exclusive (Wright's Heuristic 7). Joint voice of Nocedal and S. J. Wright (book material); framing/dating only; exclude from say-do counts. Heuristic 7 and Heuristic 9 have their own entries. Other links of this card, framing or dating only (no relation, no entry): Taste mark 1, framing (Perspectives and Software sections, p. 22, against 1999's omitted software, B005 p. 9). Research Trajectory, dating (DFO and noise a textbook section by 2006, p. 10). Roundtable Gill item, dating (reduced-Hessian SQP cut, p. 15). Honest Boundary blind spots (p. 22).
The preface commits to a typo list maintained on both authors' web pages (p. 22). Joint; shared with Wright's Heuristic 5, so it fails exclusivity. Book material: dating only.

Shared with Wright's Heuristic 6: interior methods for NLP enter the textbook once the topic 'now forms the basis of successful codes' (p. 21), after the 1999 preface had left it out as current research (p. 19; B005 p. 8). Joint, and only a pool candidate (see new_pattern_candidates).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Keep one's own live research topic out of the field text until it 'forms the basis of successful codes' (1999 omission, 2006 chapter). Pool only: joint book evidence; overlaps Wright's Heuristic 6 and Nocedal's Heuristic 9; book material alone cannot promote it.
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: 1999 preface omits IPM for NLP as current research (reprinted, p. 19; B005 p. 8); the 2006 preface adds Chapter 19 because the topic now underlies successful codes (p. 21).

transferable: Promote a topic that was left out as current research to a chapter only once it 'forms the basis of successful codes', and say why in the preface (pp. 19, 21).
When revising a text, keep the length roughly fixed and spend the effort on selecting what to include and exclude (p. 22).
End technical chapters with a 'Perspectives and Software' section that places the methods in context and names the state of the art in software (p. 22).
Keep the earlier preface verbatim and record the changes in a separate, dated preface (pp. 17-22).
coauthors: Stephen J. Wright (Computer Sciences Department, University of Wisconsin, p. 5)

quotes.text: The former topic has proved to be of great interest in applications, while the latter topic has come into its own in recent years and now forms the basis of successful codes for nonlinear programming.

After these many additions, deletions, and changes, the second edition is only slightly longer than the first, reflecting our belief that careful selection of the material to include and exclude is an important responsibility for authors of books of this type.
